o: Find k ≥ 2 factors whose product is n, minimizing max − min. Enumerate factors in non-decreasing order via trial division: at each step try every divisor d of the remainder with lo ≤ d and d² ≤ remainder (keeping factors sorted guarantees each subsequent factor is ≥ d and the final leftover completes the tuple). With n ≤ 10^5 and k ≤ 5 the search tree is tiny; track the best (difference, tuple) across leaves.
k: Generating factors in non-decreasing order (d² ≤ remainder) removes all permutation duplicates.
The last factor is forced: once k−1 factors are chosen, the remainder must be ≥ the previous factor.
Search space is bounded by divisor chains of n — negligible for n ≤ 10^5, k ≤ 5.

a.i: dfs(rem, cnt, lo, cur): if cnt == k−1, the remainder is the final factor (valid if ≥ lo) — evaluate max−min. Otherwise loop d from lo while d·d ≤ rem, recursing on rem/d with lo = d when d divides rem.
s: Base case cnt == k−1: if rem ≥ lo, score cur + [rem] and update the best.
Else for each d in [lo, √rem] dividing rem, recurse with rem/d, cnt+1, lo = d.
a.t: O(D^{k}) where D = √n divisor candidates per level — at most a few thousand nodes for n ≤ 10^5, k ≤ 5
a.sp: O(k) recursion depth plus the current tuple

w: The ascending-factor enumeration is both the correctness device (no duplicates) and the efficiency device (early termination at √rem). Pitfalls: allowing factors below the previous one (duplicate permutations, wasted time), forgetting the constraint that the final remainder must fit the ordering, and k = 2 special case (answer is the closest divisor pair around √n — worth mentioning as an interview aside). Follow-up: maximize the minimum factor instead, or return all optimal decompositions.
